--- title: "Explore your data: the tidyverse" subtitle: "The R Statistical Language · Session 2" format: revealjs: footer: A. Stamm · The R Statistical Language · Session 2 --- # Welcome back ## Where we left off {.inv} In Session 1 you built the core structures of R: ::: {.spread .spread-md .spread-evenly} - the [console]{.green}, scripts, and R as a [calculator]{.green}; - [vectors]{.green}: the workhorse, and the four ways to subset them; - [lists]{.amber}: containers of anything, reached with `[[`/`$`; - [data frames]{.indigo} & [tibbles]{.indigo}: the tables you analyse; - [reading]{.indigo} & writing data files. ::: ## Today's map {.inv} ::: {.session-arc}
1Foundations
2Explore your data
3Repeat & package
::: Session 2 is the **"explore your data"** move of the course: take rows and columns you *stored*, and turn them into understanding. - [shape it]{.green}: the pipe `|>` and `dplyr`/`tidyr`: `filter`, `select`, `mutate`, `arrange`, `group_by`/`summarise`, `pivot_*`; - [read it]{.amber}: base-R workhorses, then [ggplot2]{.amber}'s layered grammar: histograms, scatters, facets, boxplots; - [understand it]{.indigo}: the **transform → plot → interpret** loop that is Exploratory Data Analysis. ::: {.callout-desc} **The thread.** We keep the penguins data the whole session: shape it, then plot it, then read the answers back off the plots. The EDA pipeline you build here is what the *repeat & package* session and the Reproducible Workflows course will build on. ::: # Tidyverse data transformation ## The tidyverse at a glance {.inv} A **family of R packages** that work as one: consistent syntax, a shared pipe, and the same *data frame in → data frame out* flow. - [readr]{.green}: bring data *in* (`read_csv`); - [tibble]{.green}: the modern data frame; - [dplyr]{.amber}: *transform* rows, columns, groups; - [tidyr]{.amber}: *reshape*: keep data [tidy]{.amber} (`pivot_*`); - [ggplot2]{.indigo}: *visualise*; - type-focused: `purrr` (iterate), `stringr` (strings), `forcats` (factors), `lubridate` (dates). ::: {.callout-desc} **Today we master `dplyr` + `tidyr`**: the transform engine that feeds every `ggplot` and every analysis. The long tail (`purrr`, `stringr`, …) you pick up on demand. ::: ## The pipe: `|>` {.inv} The pipe `|>` sends the value on its left into the *first argument* of the function on its right: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} The pipe: top-to-bottom ```r penguins |> # raw data set dplyr::filter(species == "Adelie") |> # keep only Adelie penguins dplyr::mutate(body_mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000) # compute a new column ``` ::: Reads: penguins, THEN filter(...). One line per data processing step: easy to comment/read. ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} The nested equivalent: inside-out ```r filtered_penguins <- dplyr::filter(penguins, species == "Adelie") dplyr::mutate(filtered_penguins, body_mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000) ``` ::: ::: {.paper-card} The pipe keeps your script readable **top-to-bottom**; the nested alternative reads inside-out. The backbone of data work: one rule, **the data always goes first**. ::: ## Rows and columns: `filter` & `select` {.inv} ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Filter rows ::: {.codewindow} ::: {.editor .r name="01-filter-rows.R"} ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> # keep penguins with body mass ≥ 4000 g dplyr::filter(body_mass_g >= 4000) |> # show the first 4 penguins that meet this condition dplyr::slice(1:4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 8 species island bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g 1 Adelie Torgersen 39.2 19.6 195 4675 2 Adelie Torgersen 42 20.2 190 4250 3 Adelie Torgersen 34.6 21.1 198 4400 4 Adelie Torgersen 42.5 20.7 197 4500 # ℹ 2 more variables: sex , year ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.editor .r .fragment name="02-filter-rows.R"} ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> # conditions AND together dplyr::filter(species != "Chinstrap", !is.na(sex)) |> # show first 5 rows dplyr::slice(1:5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 8 species island bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g 1 Adelie Torgersen 39.1 18.7 181 3750 2 Adelie Torgersen 39.5 17.4 186 3800 3 Adelie Torgersen 40.3 18 195 3250 4 Adelie Torgersen 36.7 19.3 193 3450 5 Adelie Torgersen 39.3 20.6 190 3650 # ℹ 2 more variables: sex , year ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.paper-card} - [filter()](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/filter.html) keeps **rows**; - Multiple conditions in `filter` are AND-ed by default; use other logical operators (`|`, `!`, `%in%`) to combine them. ::: ### Select columns ::: {.codewindow} ::: {.editor .r name="select-columns.R"} ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> # keep these columns dplyr::select(species, island, body_mass_g) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 344 × 3 species island body_mass_g 1 Adelie Torgersen 3750 2 Adelie Torgersen 3800 3 Adelie Torgersen 3250 4 Adelie Torgersen NA 5 Adelie Torgersen 3450 6 Adelie Torgersen 3650 7 Adelie Torgersen 3625 8 Adelie Torgersen 4675 9 Adelie Torgersen 3475 10 Adelie Torgersen 4250 # ℹ 334 more rows ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.editor .r .fragment name="drop-columns.R"} ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> # drop columns whose names end with "_mm" dplyr::select(-dplyr::ends_with("_mm")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 344 × 5 species island body_mass_g sex year 1 Adelie Torgersen 3750 male 2007 2 Adelie Torgersen 3800 female 2007 3 Adelie Torgersen 3250 female 2007 4 Adelie Torgersen NA 2007 5 Adelie Torgersen 3450 female 2007 6 Adelie Torgersen 3650 male 2007 7 Adelie Torgersen 3625 female 2007 8 Adelie Torgersen 4675 male 2007 9 Adelie Torgersen 3475 2007 10 Adelie Torgersen 4250 2007 # ℹ 334 more rows ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.paper-card} - [select()](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/select.html) keeps **columns**; - helpful helpers: `starts_with()`, `ends_with()`, `contains()`, `matches()`, `everything()`. ::: ::: ## New columns: `mutate` {.inv} ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} mutate.R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> # compute the body-mass index (BMI) in kg/m² dplyr::mutate(bmi = body_mass_g / (flipper_length_mm / 100)^2) |> # keep only the columns we want to see dplyr::select(species, flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g, bmi) |> # show first 5 rows dplyr::slice(1:5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 4 species flipper_length_mm body_mass_g bmi 1 Adelie 181 3750 1145. 2 Adelie 186 3800 1098. 3 Adelie 195 3250 855. 4 Adelie NA NA NA 5 Adelie 193 3450 926. ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.paper-card} - [mutate()](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/mutate.html) computes **new columns** from existing ones, keeping everything else; - New columns are available to later steps in the **same** pipe; - You can `mutate()` several columns at once. ::: ## Recode with `case_when` {.inv} ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} case-when.R ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> # create a new column "size" based on body mass dplyr::mutate(size = dplyr::case_when( body_mass_g >= 5000 ~ "large", body_mass_g >= 3500 ~ "medium", .default = "small" )) |> # keep only the columns we want to see dplyr::select(species, body_mass_g, size) |> # show first 10 rows dplyr::slice(1:10) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 10 × 3 species body_mass_g size 1 Adelie 3750 medium 2 Adelie 3800 medium 3 Adelie 3250 small 4 Adelie NA small 5 Adelie 3450 small 6 Adelie 3650 medium 7 Adelie 3625 medium 8 Adelie 4675 medium 9 Adelie 3475 small 10 Adelie 4250 medium ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.paper-card} - [case_when()](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/case-and-replace-when.html) turns a sequence of **if…else** conditions into a new column: a tidyverse-friendly replacement for nested `ifelse`; - `case_when()` reads like a **look-up table**: each `condition ~ value` row is evaluated in order, and `.default` catches everything else; - Perfect for binning or relabelling inside a `mutate()`. ::: ## Strings with [{stringr}](https://stringr.tidyverse.org) {.inv} ::: {.codewindow} ::: {.editor .r name="01-string-manipulation.R"} ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> # species contains "inst" (Chinstrap…) dplyr::filter(stringr::str_detect(species, "inst")) |> dplyr::select(species, island, body_mass_g) |> dplyr::slice(1:14) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 14 × 3 species island body_mass_g 1 Chinstrap Dream 3500 2 Chinstrap Dream 3900 3 Chinstrap Dream 3650 4 Chinstrap Dream 3525 5 Chinstrap Dream 3725 6 Chinstrap Dream 3950 7 Chinstrap Dream 3250 8 Chinstrap Dream 3750 9 Chinstrap Dream 4150 10 Chinstrap Dream 3700 11 Chinstrap Dream 3800 12 Chinstrap Dream 3775 13 Chinstrap Dream 3700 14 Chinstrap Dream 4050 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.editor .r .fragment name="02-string-manipulation.R"} ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} species_clean <- penguins |> # "adelie" → "Adelie" dplyr::mutate( species = stringr::str_to_title(species) ) species_clean |> # "Adelie" → "Adélie" dplyr::mutate( species = stringr::str_replace( species, pattern = "Adelie", replacement = "Adélie" ) ) |> dplyr::select(species, island, body_mass_g) |> dplyr::slice(1:14) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 14 × 3 species island body_mass_g 1 Adélie Torgersen 3750 2 Adélie Torgersen 3800 3 Adélie Torgersen 3250 4 Adélie Torgersen NA 5 Adélie Torgersen 3450 6 Adélie Torgersen 3650 7 Adélie Torgersen 3625 8 Adélie Torgersen 4675 9 Adélie Torgersen 3475 10 Adélie Torgersen 4250 11 Adélie Torgersen 3300 12 Adélie Torgersen 3700 13 Adélie Torgersen 3200 14 Adélie Torgersen 3800 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.paper-card} - [{stringr}](https://stringr.tidyverse.org) gives you one consistent family for **text**: every function is `str_*` with the string first, so they all pipe; - `str_detect` pairs with `filter`, - `str_replace`/`str_to_*` with `mutate`: strings behave exactly like any tidyverse column once you use `str_*`. ::: ## Sort: `arrange` {.inv} ::: {.codewindow} ::: {.editor .r name="01-arrange-ascending.R"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> dplyr::arrange(body_mass_g) # lightest first ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 344 × 8 species island bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g 1 Chinstrap Dream 46.9 16.6 192 2700 2 Adelie Biscoe 36.5 16.6 181 2850 3 Adelie Biscoe 36.4 17.1 184 2850 4 Adelie Biscoe 34.5 18.1 187 2900 5 Adelie Dream 33.1 16.1 178 2900 6 Adelie Torgers… 38.6 17 188 2900 7 Chinstrap Dream 43.2 16.6 187 2900 8 Adelie Biscoe 37.9 18.6 193 2925 9 Adelie Dream 37.5 18.9 179 2975 10 Adelie Dream 37 16.9 185 3000 # ℹ 334 more rows # ℹ 2 more variables: sex , year ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.editor .r .fragment name="02-arrange-descending.R"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(body_mass_g), bill_length_mm) # heaviest first, ties by bill length ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 344 × 8 species island bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g 1 Gentoo Biscoe 49.2 15.2 221 6300 2 Gentoo Biscoe 59.6 17 230 6050 3 Gentoo Biscoe 48.8 16.2 222 6000 4 Gentoo Biscoe 51.1 16.3 220 6000 5 Gentoo Biscoe 45.2 16.4 223 5950 6 Gentoo Biscoe 49.8 15.9 229 5950 7 Gentoo Biscoe 48.4 14.6 213 5850 8 Gentoo Biscoe 49.3 15.7 217 5850 9 Gentoo Biscoe 55.1 16 230 5850 10 Gentoo Biscoe 48.6 16 230 5800 # ℹ 334 more rows # ℹ 2 more variables: sex , year ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.paper-card} - [arrange()](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/arrange.html) sorts the rows; - Wrap a column in [desc()](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/desc.html) to go **descending**. ::: ## Summarise by group {.inv}

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3} ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%" name="grouped-summarise.R"} ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> dplyr::group_by(species) |> dplyr::summarise( n = dplyr::n(), avg_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 3 species n avg_mass 1 Adelie 152 3701. 2 Chinstrap 68 3733. 3 Gentoo 124 5076. ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.fragment fragment-index=3} ::: {.paper-card} - [group_by()](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/group_by.html) splits the data; - [summarise()](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/summarise.html) collapses rows into **one row per group**; - [n()](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/n.html) counts rows per group; `na.rm = TRUE` skips missing values. ::: ::: ## `across()`: apply to many columns {.inv} ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} across.R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> dplyr::group_by(species) |> dplyr::summarise(dplyr::across( .cols = dplyr::where(is.numeric), .fns = \(.x) { mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE) } )) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 6 species bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g year 1 Adelie 38.8 18.3 190. 3701. 2008. 2 Chinstrap 48.8 18.4 196. 3733. 2008. 3 Gentoo 47.5 15.0 217. 5076. 2008. ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.paper-card} - [`across()`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/across.html) applies one expression to **every column that matches** a selector: no copy-pasting verbs per column; - `across(where(is.numeric), ...)` targets a whole **family** of columns at once: the bridge from "many similar lines" to programmatic thinking you'll meet again in Session 3's functions; - `\() {}` is the anonymous (lambda) function syntax to create a custom function. ::: ## Reshape with [{tidyr}](https://tidyr.tidyverse.org): `pivot_longer` & `pivot_wider` {.inv}

Lab 1: tidyverse

Lab 1: tidyverse (≈25 min). Continue in lab-1-tidyverse.R. This is the foundation: the next lab (ggplot2) and the EDA in the Reproducible Workflows course build directly on it. Labs 1–2 together are the EDA half of the pipeline: transform in lab-1, plot in lab-2.

# Plotting with base R ## Why plot? {.inv} A plot is the fastest way to *feel* your data. Anscombe's quartet is the classic proof: four data sets with nearly identical means, variances and correlations, yet plots that look nothing alike. ::: {.split-2} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/anscombe-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: The four data sets share the same slope, intercept, correlation and means; only the *plots* tell them apart. A table could not, a `hist()` of a single column would not, an illustration does. ::: {.callout-desc} **The lesson.** Look at your data before you summarise it: a single well-chosen plot often tells you more than ten summary statistics. This is the heart of *Exploratory Data Analysis*. ::: ::: ## Histograms in base R {.inv} The simplest first look at one variable: **`hist()`**. ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} hist.R ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} par(bg = "white") # opaque white figure: dark slide would hide the default black ink hist( penguins$body_mass_g, # the variable breaks = 30, # how many bins col = "steelblue", border = "white", main = "Penguin body mass (g)" # title ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.paper-card} Positron draws the plot in the **Plots** pane. `hist()` is one call, but its defaults are utilitarian. ::: ## Other base-R workhorses {.inv} ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Scatterplot ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} The rest of the base-R drawer ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} par(bg = "white") # opaque white figure so the default black ink shows on the dark slide x <- rnorm(10) y <- rnorm(10) plot(x, y) # scatter plot ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: ### Barplot ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} The rest of the base-R drawer ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} par(bg = "white") # opaque white figure so the default black ink shows on the dark slide g <- rpois(n = 10L, lambda = 1) barplot(table(g)) # counts of categories ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: ### Boxplot ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} The rest of the base-R drawer ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} par(bg = "white") # opaque white figure so the default black ink shows on the dark slide boxplot(y ~ g) # one box per group ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: ### Function plotting ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} The rest of the base-R drawer ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} par(bg = "white") # opaque white figure so the default black ink shows on the dark slide curve(sin, 0, 2*pi) # plot a function ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.paper-card} Base R can already do a lot, but its look is dated and customisation is verbose: *why* we meet **ggplot2** next. ::: ## The limit of base-R plots {.inv} ::: {.spread .spread-md .spread-evenly} Base `plot()` is fine for a quick peek. For **publication-grade** graphics (faceting, legends, themes, layered encodings), it gets unwieldy fast. That's the gap **ggplot2** fills: a single coherent *grammar*, rather than a grab-bag of functions. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} You'll implement several of these base-R plots **by hand in lab 2**, then rebuild one in ggplot2 to feel the difference. ::: # ggplot2 ## The grammar of graphics {.inv} **ggplot2** (part of the tidyverse) builds every plot from a few composable pieces: ::: {.spread .spread-md .spread-evenly} - **[data]{.green}**: a data frame (usually a tibble); - **[aesthetics]{.green}** (`aes`): *which variables* map to *which visual channel* (x, y, colour, size, fill, …); - **[geometries]{.amber}** (`geom_*`): *how* the data are drawn (points, lines, bars, histograms, …); - **[facets]{.indigo}**: small multiples, splitting by a variable; - **[scales/themes]{.indigo}**: the polish. ::: ## The first ggplot {.inv} Every plot starts with `ggplot(data = , mapping = aes(...))`, then adds layers with `+`: ::: {.split-2} 
ggplot(
    data = penguins, 
    mapping = aes(x = body_mass_g)
  ) + 
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, color = "white")
::: {.plot-stack} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="1"} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="2"} ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.paper-card .fragment} This is the *same histogram* we drew in base R, but now each piece is explicit and easy to extend. ::: ## Scatter: two continuous variables {.inv} Mapping variables to `x` and `y`, and a third to `color`: ::: {.split-2} 
ggplot(
    data = penguins,
    mapping = aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)
  ) + 
  geom_point(aes(color = species), alpha = 0.7) + 
  theme_dark() + 
  labs(
    title = "Body mass variation with flipper length",
    caption = "Data from the {palmerpengins} package.",
    x = "Flipper Length (mm)", 
    y = "Body Mass (g)", 
    color = "Species"
  )
::: {.plot-stack} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="1"} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="2"} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="3"} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-23-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="4"} ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.paper-card .fragment} **Read it aloud.** "Body mass grows with flipper length", and each species clusters in its own region of this space. That's a finding you'd never see from `summary()`. ::: ## One variable per facet {.inv} **Faceting** splits the plot into small multiples: one per level of a variable: ::: {.split-2} 
ggplot(
    data = penguins, 
    mapping = aes(x = body_mass_g)
  ) + 
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 25, 
    fill = "#2E7D6B", 
    color = "#17251F"
  ) + 
  facet_wrap(
    facets = vars(species), 
    ncol = 1
  ) + 
  theme_dark()
::: {.plot-stack} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="1"} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-25-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="2"} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-26-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="3"} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-27-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="4"} ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.paper-card .fragment} Different species have *different* distributions of body mass: a comparison that's hard to see in one pooled histogram. ::: ## Boxplots for groups {.inv} Categorical `x` + continuous `y`: ::: {.split-2} 
ggplot(
    data = penguins, 
    mapping = aes(x = species, y = bill_length_mm, fill = species)
  ) + 
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.8) + 
  theme_dark() + 
  theme(legend.position = "none")
::: {.plot-stack} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-28-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="1"} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-29-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="2"} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-30-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="3"} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-31-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="4"} ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.paper-card .fragment} A boxplot shows the median, the box (IQR) and outliers at a glance: ideal for comparing a numeric variable *across groups*. ::: ## Order factors with [{forcats}](https://forcats.tidyverse.org) {.inv} [{forcats}](https://forcats.tidyverse.org) lets you **reorder** those levels so graphs tell the story you want: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%" name="fct-reorder.R"} ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> dplyr::mutate(species = forcats::fct_reorder( .f = species, .x = bill_length_mm, .fun = median, na.rm = TRUE )) |> ggplot(mapping = aes( x = species, y = bill_length_mm, fill = species )) + geom_boxplot() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-32-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.paper-card} `fct_reorder()` puts the *highest median first* on the axis: order becomes part of your message. `fct_relevel`/`fct_lump` fine-tune and collapse rare levels. ::: ## Layers compose {.inv} An important ggplot2 habit: plots are built from **many layers**. For example, scatter + a smooth trend: ::: {.split-2} 
ggplot(
    data = penguins, 
    mapping = aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)
  ) + 
  geom_point(aes(color = species), alpha = 0.6) + 
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm", 
    se = FALSE, 
    color = "#E8A33D", 
    linewidth = 1
  ) + 
  theme_dark()
::: {.plot-stack} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-33-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="1"} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-34-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="2"} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-35-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="3"} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-36-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="4"} ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.paper-card .fragment} `geom_point()` and `geom_smooth()` *layer* on the same plot, each with its own mapping. This layering is what makes ggplot2 so expressive. ::: ## A grammar, not a menu {.inv} ::: {.spread .spread-md .spread-evenly} The power is **consistency**: you learn a few verbs (`geom_point`, `geom_bar`, `geom_histogram`, `facet_wrap`, `aes`) and combine them, instead of memorising a different function per plot type. There's a gallery of extensions (e.g. `{ggpubr}`, `{patchwork}`, `{plotly}` for interactivity): ::: ::: {.callout-desc} We'll run a *ggplot2 build-up* live: from a bare histogram to a faceted, titled, themed figure in a handful of added lines. Watch how small edits compound. ::: ## Your turn: plotting {.paper} ::: {.paper-card} 1. Load penguins with `read_csv("penguins.csv")`. 2. Base R: scatter `body_mass_g` vs `flipper_length_mm`, by species. 3. ggplot2: same plot with `color = species`. 4. `hist()` of `body_mass_g` + `facet_wrap(~ species)`. 5. Which approach would you reach for? :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
